facts.text: Before thermometers, doctors judged fever by feeling the skin with a hand.
Galileo made an air thermoscope around 1600: a bulb and tube standing in water.
The water level in the thermoscope moved as the trapped air warmed or cooled.
The thermoscope had no scale, and air-pressure changes also moved the water.
In the early 1600s (about 1612), Santorio added a scale to the device.
Santorio placed the bulb in patients’ mouths; it is the first known clinical use.
Thermometers used by doctors in the mid-1800s were large and could need 20 minutes.
Thomas Allbutt, an English doctor in Leeds, designed a short clinical thermometer.
Allbutt’s thermometer was first made in 1867; it was about 15 cm (six inches) long.
Allbutt’s thermometer gave a reading in about five minutes.
Glass thermometers with mercury are not recommended: glass breaks and mercury is a poison.
Electronic (digital) thermometers are most often suggested; probes go in the mouth or armpit.
Ear thermometers are easy to use but some users find them less accurate than probes.
With an ear thermometer, the button is held for about one second.
Pulling the outer ear back straightens the ear canal toward the eardrum.
Wait at least 1 hour after heavy exercise or a hot bath before measuring.
Wait 20 to 30 minutes after a hot or cold drink before measuring.
Body temperature changes during the day and is often highest in the evening.
A temperature over 38 °C (100.4 °F) most often indicates a fever.
